content: Palatine tonsils are the visible tonsils located at the back of the throat. Tonsillitis refers to the inflammation of these tonsils, which often, but not always, results in symptoms such as a sore throat and fever. In chronic cases, surgical removal of the tonsils, known as tonsillectomy, may be necessary. The palatine tonsils play a significant role in local immunity. Tonsillar B cells are capable of maturing to produce all five major immunoglobulin (Ig) classes. When stimulated in vitro with mitogens or specific antigens, these B cells generate antibodies against pathogens such as diphtheria toxoid, poliovirus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, and the lipopolysaccharide of Escherichia coli. Most of the IgA produced by tonsillar B cells in vitro is in the form of 7S monomers, although a notable proportion may exist as 10S dimeric IgA. In addition to humoral immunity, the palatine tonsils elicit a robust T-cell response following antigenic stimulation. For instance, natural infection or intranasal immunization with live attenuated rubella virus vaccine has been shown to prime tonsillar lymphocytes more effectively than subcutaneous vaccination. Similarly, natural infection with varicella-zoster virus stimulates tonsillar lymphocytes more effectively than peripheral blood lymphocytes. However, combined tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy have been observed to significantly impair the local IgA response in nasopharyngeal fluid against poliovirus, correlating with an increased incidence of paralytic poliomyelitis post-surgery. These findings underscore the critical role of the tonsils in defending against bacterial and viral infections and in supporting regional mucosal immunity, particularly in response to intranasal vaccines. The palatine tonsils are continuously engaged in local immune responses to microorganisms. However, persistent stimulation of tonsillar lymphocytes may overwhelm their capacity to respond to other antigens, potentially impairing the immune response, especially in cases of recurrent tonsillitis. Once this immunological dysfunction occurs, the tonsils may lose their ability to provide adequate local protection and fail to reinforce the secretory immune system of the upper respiratory tract. Cytokines, which are immunomodulatory proteins or glycoproteins, play a crucial role in regulating immune responses. They influence target cells by activating genes that lead to mitotic division, growth, differentiation, migration, or apoptosis. Cytokines are produced by various cell types in response to both antigen-specific and non-antigen-specific stimuli. The balance between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines significantly impacts the clinical outcomes of infectious, autoimmune, and malignant diseases. Studies of cytokine profiles in tonsillar tissue provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying these disorders and the interactions between T and B lymphocytes and other immunocompetent cells. The cytokine network represents a sophisticated regulatory system essential for overcoming microbial defense strategies. Both Th1 and Th2 cytokines, as well as their mRNA, are detectable in conditions such as tonsillar hypertrophy and recurrent tonsillitis, highlighting the active immunological role of the palatine tonsils. These tissues persistently harbor microbial antigens, even in asymptomatic individuals, which may reflect the ontogeny of the immune system. Anatomically, the palatine tonsils are part of the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) and are located at the entrance to the upper respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts. This strategic position allows them to protect the body from exogenous materials entering through mucosal sites. However, this also makes them a potential focus for infections. The palatine tonsils are a key immunocompetent tissue in the oropharynx and form part of Waldeyer's ring, which includes the nasopharyngeal tonsil (adenoid), paired tubal tonsils, paired palatine tonsils, and the lingual tonsil. In children, the tonsils are common sites of infection, leading to acute or chronic tonsillitis. The role of persistent infection in causing tonsillar hypertrophy remains uncertain. Tonsillectomy is one of the most frequently performed major surgeries in children, but its indications are complicated by debates over the benefits of removing chronically infected tissue versus the potential harm of eliminating an important immune-inductive site. A rational decision regarding tonsillectomy requires an understanding of the immunological potential of normal palatine tonsils and a comparison with the changes observed in chronically diseased tonsils. The palatine tonsils contain an extensive system of crypts, which significantly increase their internal surface area. These crypts are lined by stratified squamous epithelium and extend deep into the tonsils, forming a complex network of canals surrounded by blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and germinal centers. The crypts serve as a forward sentry for the immune system, exposing immune cells to infectious organisms introduced into the body via food or other ingested materials. However, the crypts can also become a site for bacterial colonization, leading to the formation of solidified plugs or stones known as tonsilloliths. These structures can cause bad breath, obstruct the normal flow of pus, and irritate the throat, often giving sufferers the sensation of a foreign object in their throat. The pathogenesis of infectious or inflammatory diseases in the tonsils is likely related to their anatomical location and immune function. Viral infections with secondary bacterial invasion may initiate chronic disease, but environmental factors, host characteristics, antibiotic use, ecological considerations, and diet may also contribute. Acute tonsillitis, the most common manifestation of tonsillar disease, is characterized by sore throat, fever, and dysphagia. The tonsils may appear erythematous and may or may not exhibit exudates. Recurrent tonsillitis is variably defined as multiple episodes of acute tonsillitis over a specified period. Tonsillar hypertrophy, the enlargement of the tonsils without a history of inflammation, is the most common reason for tonsillectomy, particularly in cases of obstructive sleep disturbances. Symptoms of obstructive tonsillar hypertrophy include loud snoring, nocturnal choking, frequent awakenings, restless sleep, dysphagia, daytime hypersomnolence, and behavioral changes.
